{{Short description|Mathematical function}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''algebraic function''' is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] that satisfies a [[polynomial equation]]. Thus an equation of the following form holds:
<math display="block">a_n(x)f(x)^n + a_{n-1}(x)f(x)^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1(x)f(x) + a_0(x) = 0</math>
where the <math>a_k(x)</math> are polynomials (not all zero). Basic examples of algebraic functions are [[polynomial function]]s, [[rational function]]s, the [[nth root]] function, and functions obtained from these by composition and algebraic operations (addition, multiplication, subtraction, and division).  Thus an example of an algebraic function is the function <math>f(x) = \sqrt{1-x^2}</math> (for <math>-1<x<1</math>), whose graph is the top half of the standard [[unit circle]].  This function satisfies <math>x^2+f(x)^2-1=0</math>.  Algebraic functions are contrasted with [[transcendental functions]], such as the [[exponential function]], [[logarithm]], and the [[trigonometric function]]s.

Algebraic functions are usually treated more generally as [[multivalued function]]s. The example of <math>x^2+y^2-1=0</math> illustrates this, since it includes both the top semicircle <math>y=\sqrt{1-x^2}</math> and bottom semicircle <math>y=-\sqrt{1-x^2}</math> in the same package. Algebraic functions are most often studied over the [[complex number]]s.  Formally, an algebraic function over the complex numbers is defined to be a multivalued function <math>y</math> satisfying a polynomial equation
<math display="block">P(x,y) = 0</math>
where <math>P(x,y)</math> is an [[irreducible polynomial]] of two variables, having positive degree in <math>y</math> and complex coefficients.<ref name="Bliss2004">{{cite book
 | last = Bliss
 | first = Gilbert Ames
 | author-link = Gilbert Ames Bliss
 | title = Algebraic Functions
 | publisher = Dover Publications
 | series = Dover Phoenix Editions
 | year = 2004
 | isbn = 978-0-486-49568-2
 | orig-year = 1933
}}, Chapter II.</ref> The example of <math>x^2+y^2-1=0</math> can be expressed as having the two single-valued [[Branch (mathematical analysis)|branches]], <math>y=\sqrt{1-x^2}</math> and <math>y=-\sqrt{1-x^2}</math>, with [[branch point]]s where the two branches come together, at <math>x=\pm 1</math>. This particular function can be written using finitely many algebraic operations and extraction of nth roots, but this is not generally the case such as with the [[Bring radical]]. Over the complex numbers, algebraic functions have local [[holomorphic]] branches away from finitely many branch points and [[pole (complex analysis)|poles]], and are naturally studied as [[meromorphic function]]s on compact [[Riemann surfaces]].<ref name="Forster1981">{{citation
 | last = Forster
 | first = Otto
 | title = Lectures on Riemann Surfaces
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Graduate Texts in Mathematics
 | volume = 81
 | year = 1981
 | isbn = 978-0-387-90617-1
}}, Section I.8.</ref>

More generally, over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>K</math>, an algebraic function in one variable <math>x</math> is defined algebraically as an element [[algebraic extension|algebraic]] over the [[rational function field]] <math>K(x)</math>. Equivalently, it satisfies a polynomial equation of positive degree in <math>y</math>,
: <math>a_n(x)y^n+a_{n-1}(x)y^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0(x)=0,</math>
where the coefficients <math>a_i(x)</math> are polynomials in <math>x</math> with coefficients in <math>K</math>. If the irreducible defining polynomial has degree <math>n</math> in <math>y</math>, the algebraic function is said to have degree <math>n</math>.

An '''algebraic function in <math>m</math> variables''' over <math>K</math> is an element algebraic over the field of [[rational function]]s <math>K(x_1,\ldots,x_m)</math>. Equivalently, it satisfies a polynomial equation
:<math>p(y,x_1,x_2,\dots,x_m)=0.</math>
In one variable, algebraic functions are closely related to [[algebraic curve]]s and their [[function field (algebraic geometry)|function fields]]; in the [[separable extension|separable]] case, they may also be studied via finite or [[ramified cover]]s of the [[projective line]].<ref name="Fulton2008">{{cite web
 | last = Fulton
 | first = William
 | author-link = William Fulton (mathematician)
 | title = Algebraic Curves: An Introduction to Algebraic Geometry
 | year = 2008
 | url = https://users.math.msu.edu/users/magyarp/Math419H/Fulton-Alg-Curves.pdf
}}</ref>

== Algebraic functions in one variable ==
===Basic examples===
Polynomial and rational functions are algebraic. A polynomial function <math>y=p(x)</math> satisfies
:<math>y-p(x)=0.</math>
A rational function <math>y=p(x)/q(x)</math> satisfies
:<math>q(x)y-p(x)=0,</math>
with poles at the zeros of <math>q</math>. More generally, the <math>n</math>th root of a polynomial or rational function is algebraic, since it satisfies an equation such as
:<math>y^n-p(x)=0.</math>

Many elementary algebraic functions can be obtained from rational functions by algebraic operations and extraction of roots. However, algebraic functions are more general than functions expressible by radicals. By Galois theory, roots of a general polynomial equation of degree five or higher cannot be expressed by radicals.

Where a local inverse branch of an algebraic function exists, it is again algebraic. More generally, if <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> satisfy a polynomial relation <math>P(x,y)=0</math>, then interchanging the roles of <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> gives an algebraic correspondence whose branches include the local inverse branches. The solution set <math>P(x,y)=0</math> is an algebraic curve; away from exceptional points, its local branches may be represented as graphs over the <math>x</math>-line.

=== The role of complex numbers ===

From an algebraic perspective, complex numbers enter quite naturally into the study of algebraic functions.  First of all, by the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]], the complex numbers are an [[algebraically closed field]]. Hence, for each value of <math>x</math> for which <math>p(x,y)</math> is a nonconstant polynomial of degree <math>n</math> in <math>y</math>, the equation <math>p(x,y)=0</math> has <math>n</math> complex roots counted with multiplicity. Exceptional values of <math>x</math>, such as zeros of the leading coefficient or of the [[discriminant]], are responsible for poles, multiple roots, and branch points.

[[Image:y^3-xy+1=0.png|thumb|A graph of three branches of the algebraic function ''y'', where ''y''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''xy''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, over the domain 3/2<sup>2/3</sup> < ''x'' < 50.]]
Furthermore, even if one is ultimately interested in real algebraic functions, there may be no means to express the function in terms of addition, multiplication, division and taking ''nth'' roots without resorting to complex numbers (see [[casus irreducibilis]]).  For example, consider the algebraic function determined by the equation

:<math>y^3-xy+1=0.\,</math>

Using the [[cubic formula]], we get

:<math>
y=-\frac{2x}{\sqrt[3]{-108+12\sqrt{81-12x^3}}}+\frac{\sqrt[3]{-108+12\sqrt{81-12x^3}}}{6}.
</math>

For <math>x\le \frac{3}{\sqrt[3]{4}},</math> the square root is real and the cubic root is thus well defined, providing the unique real root. On the other hand, for <math>x>\frac{3}{\sqrt[3]{4}},</math> the square root is not real, and one has to choose, for the square root, either non-real square root. Thus the cubic root has to be chosen among three non-real numbers. If the same choices are done in the two terms of the formula, the three choices for the cubic root provide the three branches shown, in the accompanying image.

It may be proven that there is no way to express this function in terms of ''nth'' roots using real numbers only, even though the resulting function is real-valued on the domain of the graph shown.

On a more significant theoretical level, using complex numbers allows one to use the powerful techniques of [[complex analysis]] to discuss algebraic functions.  In particular, the [[argument principle]] can be used to show that any algebraic function is in fact an [[analytic function]], at least in the multiple-valued sense.

Formally, let ''p''(''x'', ''y'') be a complex polynomial in the complex variables ''x'' and ''y''.  Suppose that
''x''<sub>0</sub> ∈ '''C''' is such that the polynomial ''p''(''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''y'') of ''y'' has ''n'' distinct zeros.  We shall show that the algebraic function is analytic in a [[Neighborhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] of ''x''<sub>0</sub>.  Choose a system of ''n'' non-overlapping discs Δ<sub>''i''</sub> containing each of these zeros.  Then by the argument principle

:<math>\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial\Delta_i} \frac{p_y(x_0,y)}{p(x_0,y)}\,dy = 1.</math>

By continuity, this also holds for all ''x'' in a neighborhood of ''x''<sub>0</sub>.  In particular, ''p''(''x'', ''y'') has only one root in Δ<sub>''i''</sub>, given by the [[residue theorem]]:

:<math>f_i(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial\Delta_i} y\frac{p_y(x,y)}{p(x,y)}\,dy</math>

which is an analytic function.

===Branch points and Puiseux series===
At a critical value, the local branches need not be single-valued functions of <math>x</math>. Instead, after introducing a local parameter <math>t</math> with <math>x-x_0=t^e</math>, the branches can be represented by convergent [[Puiseux series]]<ref name="Bliss2004"/>
<math display="block">
y=\sum_{j=j_0}^{\infty} a_j t^j
=\sum_{j=j_0}^{\infty} a_j (x-x_0)^{j/e}.
</math>
The integer <math>e</math> describes the ramification of the branch. Algebraic functions have no singularities other than poles and algebraic branch points.

=== Monodromy ===
Note that the foregoing proof of analyticity derived an expression for a system of ''n'' different '''function elements''' ''f''<sub>''i''{{space|hair}}</sub>(''x''), provided that ''x'' is not a '''critical value''' of the projection to the <math>x</math>-line. A critical value is a value of <math>x</math> for which the number of distinct zeros of <math>p(x,y)</math> is smaller than the degree of <math>p</math> in <math>y</math>; this occurs only where the leading coefficient in <math>y</math> or the [[discriminant]] vanishes. Hence there are only finitely many such values ''c''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''c''<sub>''m''</sub>.

A close analysis of the properties of the function elements ''f''<sub>''i''</sub> near the critical values can be used to show that the  [[monodromy theorem|monodromy cover]] is [[Ramification (mathematics)|ramified]] over the critical values (and possibly the [[Riemann sphere|point at infinity]]).  Thus the [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic]] extension of the ''f''<sub>''i''</sub> has at worst algebraic poles and ordinary algebraic branchings over the critical values.

Note that, away from the critical values, we have

:<math>p(x,y) = a_n(x)(y-f_1(x))(y-f_2(x))\cdots(y-f_n(x))</math>

since the ''f''<sub>''i''</sub> are by definition the distinct zeros of ''p''.  Analytic continuation of the local branches around loops avoiding the critical values permutes the branches; these permutations form the [[monodromy group]] of the algebraic function. (The [[monodromy action]] on the [[universal covering space]] is related but different notion in the theory of [[Riemann surface]]s.)

Algebraically, if <math>L</math> is the [[splitting field]] of <math>p(x,y)</math> over <math>\mathbb C(x)</math>, equivalently the [[Galois closure]] of the extension generated by one branch, then the [[Galois group]] <math>\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb C(x))</math> acts by permuting the roots <math>f_1,\ldots,f_n</math>. Under the correspondence between finite branched covers of the [[Riemann sphere]] and finite extensions of <math>\mathbb C(x)</math>, this Galois group is identified with the monodromy group of the covering. Thus the monodromy action realizes the Galois group of the splitting field as a permutation group on the branches.

== Closure properties ==

Algebraic functions are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and composition, wherever the operations are defined. Algebraically, this follows from the fact that if <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> are algebraic over <math>K(x)</math>, then the field <math>K(x,u,v)</math> is a finite algebraic extension of <math>K(x)</math>; hence any rational expression in <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> is again algebraic over <math>K(x)</math>.  Similarly, if <math>f</math> is algebraic over <math>K(x)</math> and <math>g</math> is algebraic over <math>K(t)</math>, then, under suitable interpretation of branches, <math>f(g(t))</math> is again algebraic. Equivalently, if algebraic functions are regarded as algebraic correspondences on the projective line, the composite correspondence is again algebraic. If <math>P(x,y)=0</math> and <math>Q(t,x)=0</math> define two such correspondences, then their composite is contained in the algebraic relation obtained by eliminating <math>x</math>, for instance by the resultant
:<math>\operatorname{Res}_x(Q(t,x),P(x,y))=0.</math><ref>{{cite conference
 | last1 = Kozen
 | first1 = Dexter
 | author-link1 = Dexter Kozen
 | last2 = Landau
 | first2 = Susan
 | author-link2 = Susan Landau
 | last3 = Zippel
 | first3 = Richard
 | title = Decomposition of algebraic functions
 | book-title = Algorithmic Number Theory
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | volume = 877
 | publisher = Springer
 | year = 1994
 | pages = 99–112
 | doi = 10.1007/3-540-58691-1_46
}}</ref>

On a nonsingular branch, the derivative of an algebraic function is also algebraic. Differentiating <math>P(x,y)=0</math> implicitly gives
:<math>y'=-{P_x(x,y)\over P_y(x,y)},</math>
where this expression is valid away from points at which <math>P_y=0</math>. By contrast, an antiderivative of an algebraic function need not be algebraic. Integrals of algebraic functions lead more generally to [[Abelian integral]]s, such as [[elliptic integral]]s.<ref name="LangAlgebraicAbelian">{{cite book
 | last = Lang
 | first = Serge
 | author-link = Serge Lang
 | title = Introduction to Algebraic and Abelian Functions
 | edition = 2nd
 | series = Graduate Texts in Mathematics
 | volume = 89
 | publisher = Springer
 | year = 1982
 | isbn = 978-0-387-90710-9
}}</ref>

== History ==

The ideas surrounding algebraic functions go back at least as far as [[René Descartes]].  The first discussion of algebraic functions appears to have been in [[Edward Waring]]'s 1794 ''An Essay on the Principles of Human Knowledge'' in which he writes:
:let a quantity denoting the ordinate, be an algebraic function of the abscissa ''x'', by the common methods of division and extraction of roots, reduce it into an infinite series ascending or descending according to the dimensions of ''x'', and then find the integral of each of the resulting terms.
